procedural_history.impugned_order: Order of the Calcutta High Court dated March 28, 1968, quashing the processes issued against the three accused persons.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings:
1. The Magistrate dismissed the complaint under section 203 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
2. The complainant moved the Sessions Judge, Purulia, against the order of dismissal.
3. A reference was made to the Calcutta High Court.
4. A Single Judge of the Calcutta High Court accepted the reference, set aside the order of the Magistrate, and sent the case back for proceeding in accordance with law.
5. The High Court, in a petition to quash the issue of process, held that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate had no right to issue process since he was not the Magistrate who had taken cognizance of the offence and also observed that the evidence in the case came from tainted sources.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave against the High Court's judgment. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision to quash the process against T. Ganguly.

issue.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, who has not taken cognizance of an offence and to whom the case has not been transferred, has the authority to issue process under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: A criminal complaint was filed, and Magistrate Shri S. K. Ganguly took cognizance of the case.
After a judicial enquiry, Magistrate Ganguly concluded that a prima facie case was made out and submitted a report to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.
The Sub-Divisional Magistrate (Shri S. Sarkar), upon receiving the report, issued the process against the accused.
Crucially, there was no formal order transferring the case from Magistrate Ganguly, who had taken cognizance, to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate who issued the process.
law: Under Section 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), the Magistrate who takes cognizance of an offence is empowered to issue process.
Under Section 202 of the Cr.P.C., a Magistrate to whom a case has been formally transferred by the Magistrate who took cognizance can also issue process.
The issuance of process is a matter for judicial determination that must be performed by a magistrate with the proper authority under one of these two sections.
application: The Court analyzed the two legal pathways for a magistrate to issue process: either by taking cognizance themselves (Sec. 204) or by having the case officially transferred to them (Sec. 202).
In this instance, the Sub-Divisional Magistrate who issued the process had not taken cognizance of the offence; Magistrate Ganguly had.
Furthermore, the case was never formally transferred from Magistrate Ganguly to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.
Because the Sub-Divisional Magistrate met neither of the legal requirements, he acted without the necessary authority.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a Magistrate who has not taken cognizance of an offence and to whom the case has not been transferred lacks the authority to issue process. Since the Magistrate who issued the process in this case fell into this category, the Court affirmed the High Court's decision to quash the process.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, under its inherent powers (Section 561-A Cr.P.C.), can examine the question of whether there is any legal evidence to support the issuance of process.

facts: The appellant argued that the High Court should not have examined the question of whether a prima facie case was established when it was asked to quash the issuance of process.
The High Court had observed that the evidence in the case came from "tainted sources" and was not reliable.
law: The Supreme Court identified Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure as the source of the High Court's inherent power to examine such issues.
application: The Supreme Court directly stated that the High Court, under its inherent powers in Section 561-A, can indeed examine the question of whether there is any legal evidence to support the case.

It interpreted the High Court's finding that the evidence was from "tainted sources" and unreliable as being equivalent to a finding of "no case to go to the jury," which is a determination about the legal sufficiency of the evidence.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was within its rights under Section 561-A of the Code of Criminal Procedure to go into the question of whether there was any legal evidence to support the issuance of process.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a Magistrate, who has not taken cognizance of an offence and to whom the case has not been transferred, has the authority to issue process under the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The appellant implicitly argued that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate's order to issue process was valid. This was a challenge to the High Court's finding that the order was without jurisdiction.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (Shri S. Sarkar) had no authority to issue process under Section 204 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as he was not the Magistrate who had taken cognizance of the offence (that was Shri S. K. Ganguly).

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, under its inherent powers (Section 561-A Cr.P.C.), can examine the question of whether there is any legal evidence to support the issuance of process.
appellant_arguments: The appellant, by appealing the High Court's decision, implicitly argued against the High Court's intervention, which included its observation on the quality of the evidence. The argument would be that examining the evidence as coming from 'tainted sources' was premature at the stage of issuing process.
respondent_arguments: The respondent argued that the High Court could exercise its inherent powers to quash proceedings if the evidence on which the process was issued was insufficient or came from 'tainted sources', in order to prevent an abuse of the process of the court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The power to issue a process against an accused is restricted to either the magistrate who has taken cognizance of the offense or a magistrate to whom the case has been formally transferred; a magistrate who has done neither is not competent to issue the process.
obiter: Under section 561A of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court has the authority to determine if there is any legal evidence to support a complaint.
The complainant must be examined under section 200 of the Code of Criminal Procedure in cases where a magistrate has taken cognizance or where a case has been transferred to another magistrate.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Court held that the issuance of process against the accused was invalid because the Magistrate who issued it had neither taken cognizance of the offence himself nor had the case been formally transferred to him, which are the only two circumstances under which a Magistrate can issue process according to the Code of Criminal Procedure. The Court also affirmed that the High Court, under its inherent powers, is entitled to examine whether there is any legal evidence to support the issuance of process in order to prevent an abuse of the court's process.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 204, Cr.P.C., the Magistrate who takes cognizance of an offence is the one who can issue process.
Under Section 202, Cr.P.C., a Magistrate to whom a case has been transferred can issue process.

Under Section 561-A, Cr.P.C., the High Court has the inherent power to go into the question as to whether there is any legal evidence to support a prosecution, and can quash proceedings if there is none, which the court described as a 'no case to go to the jury' situation.
why_appellant_lost: The Magistrate who issued the process had not taken cognizance of the offence.
There was no order transferring the case to the Magistrate who issued the process from the Magistrate who had taken cognizance.

The appellant's contention that the High Court should not have examined the evidence was incorrect, as the High Court has the power under Section 561-A Cr.P.C. to determine if any legal evidence exists to support the process.
why_respondent_won: The Sub-Divisional Magistrate who issued the process lacked jurisdiction because he was not the Magistrate who had taken cognizance of the offence, nor was he one to whom the case had been transferred.

The High Court correctly exercised its inherent power under Section 561-A Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings by examining the evidence and finding it came from 'tainted sources', which amounted to a finding that there was no legal evidence.
policy_considerations: The issuance of process is a matter for judicial determination, not an administrative one. The requirement that the process be issued by the Magistrate who has taken cognizance or to whom the case is transferred ensures that the decision is made by the judicial officer who has properly examined the complainant and is seized of the case.
